subject: Cab Calloway — Minnie the Moocher (Blue Brothers)
headline: Cab Calloway Gets His Big Number Back
article:
By the time Cab Calloway sings “Minnie the Moocher” in The Blues Brothers, the song is nearly half a century old. The owned video is not a generic Calloway listing: its title and album point to the 1980 soundtrack, and the picture shows Calloway in white, fronting a band on a deliberately theatrical set.

That distinction matters. “Minnie the Moocher” had been Calloway’s signature since the early 1930s, but John Landis’s film does not present the number as a sepia flashback. The production reportedly resisted Calloway’s idea for a disco variation and steered the scene toward a big-band arrangement instead. Calloway’s entrance, the band’s formal line, and the camera’s attention to his body turn the performance into a handoff between eras: the film’s young revivalists make room for the man who already knew how to command a crowd.

The title is therefore doing useful work, even if it is imprecise as a song label. This file represents Calloway’s return to his best-known number through a 1980 film performance—not “St. James Infirmary Blues,” and not a newly discovered studio take. Minnie is the point: a song old enough to be history, staged as if it had just walked through the door.
angle: The film did not treat Calloway as a museum piece: it rebuilt his signature number as a large, live-feeling set piece and let a new audience meet the performer inside the song.

subject: Buddy Holly — Not Fade Away and Peggy Sue
headline: One File, Two Buddy Holly Songs
article:
The useful fact about this Buddy Holly file is hiding in plain sight: it names two songs. “Not Fade Away” and “Peggy Sue” are not alternate titles for one performance, and the 1956 year in the player’s description cannot safely serve as the release year for either. Both songs are generally documented as 1957 recordings.

That makes the asset a small lesson in how rock history gets packaged. “Not Fade Away” belongs to Holly and the Crickets and carries a co-writing credit associated with Norman Petty; “Peggy Sue” is tied to Holly, Jerry Allison, and Petty, with the song’s title famously connected to Allison’s girlfriend. Later compilations routinely place such signatures beside one another, turning a career into a neat shelf. The filename does the same thing, but more honestly: it says this is a two-song performance or program.

The picture complicates the label further. A sampled frame shows a period microphone and a sung performance, but it does not by itself prove that the footage is Holly, nor whether the file is archival, dramatized, or assembled from more than one source. The right story is not a forced identity. It is the collision of two songs—and the warning that a compilation year is not a recording date.
angle: The asset is more interesting as a compact Holly double feature than as a mislabelled single-song page: one title contains two different pieces of the Holly myth.

subject: Big Band — Rhapsody in Blue
headline: Rhapsody in Blue Was Built to Be Recast
article:
“Rhapsody in Blue” arrived with a famous name attached to it, but not with a single permanent sound. George Gershwin’s piece was commissioned by Paul Whiteman and premiered in 1924 with Gershwin at the piano. Ferde Grofé orchestrated the accompaniment, and later versions helped turn the work into something many listeners recognize as a full concert showpiece.

The owned file makes that history visible without identifying its orchestra. In a monochrome, Warner Archive-marked frame, a featured clarinetist stands before a large ensemble: piano in the foreground, brass and rhythm instruments behind him, the arrangement doing the work of translating Gershwin’s blue notes into a staged band performance. The player year, 1948, and the album phrase about a Bay Big Band and the Brussels World’s Fair are valuable leads, but neither proves that this is the original event, the named orchestra, or even the composition’s date.

That uncertainty does not weaken the subject. It points to the central story. “Rhapsody in Blue” has survived partly by being recast—by Whiteman, by orchestral arrangers, by bands, by broadcasters, and by performers who keep negotiating the border between jazz and the concert hall. Here, the missing name is less important than the visible argument: this music keeps changing clothes without losing its outline.
angle: Rhapsody in Blue is a work whose identity is partly its repeated rearrangement; the unknown band is not a gap to fill with a guess but part of the media object’s history.

subject: Animation — Vintage Banned Cartoons
headline: “Banned Cartoons” Is a Question, Not a Title
article:
The first thing this file tells us is what it does not tell us. “Vintage Banned Cartoons” is a broad label, not a title list. A sampled frame shows a black-and-white animated party scene, but it does not identify the cartoon, studio, year, or the reason anyone might have withdrawn it. The 1950 attached to the file is a useful lead, not proof of the image’s date.

There is real history behind the category. Animation has been altered by changing standards, local censorship, syndication decisions, and later attempts to keep offensive material out of ordinary television circulation. The documented Censored Eleven, for example, were Warner Bros. shorts withdrawn from syndication in 1968 because of racist portrayals. But that fact belongs to those identified films; it cannot be transferred to an unnamed frame simply because the filename says “banned.”

That restraint is the interesting angle. A compilation like this is an archival prompt: name the films, locate their sources, and distinguish “withdrawn,” “edited,” “unavailable,” and “banned,” which are not interchangeable conditions. Until that work is done, the responsible description is modest but useful: an owned vintage-animation compilation whose subject is censorship, with its individual contents still unverified. The blank space is part of the research, not a license to fill it with folklore.
angle: The honest story is about the danger of the label itself: a compilation called banned is an invitation to investigate, not permission to invent a censorship history.

subject: Paul Simon — You Can Call Me Al
headline: The Video That Makes Paul Simon Look Like Chevy Chase
article:
The joke in “You Can Call Me Al” begins before the song does. Paul Simon sits beside Chevy Chase, and the video makes the taller comedian appear to own the lead vocal while Simon supplies the deadpan counterpoint. Chase lip-syncs Simon’s part; Simon mouths the backing vocal and keeps introducing instruments as if the studio has become a very small vaudeville stage.

The arrangement underneath the gag is unusually busy. Simon recorded the song at New York’s Hit Factory in April 1986 for Graceland, with a horn arrangement by Rob Mounsey and a bass line built around a descending figure played by Bakithi Kumalo. The single did not simply arrive and explode: after an initial number 44 appearance on the Billboard Hot 100, it returned and climbed to number 23 in 1987 as the album’s audience grew.

That delayed chart life fits the video’s trick. It is accessible on first glance—a famous comedian pretending to sing—but its pleasure comes from watching the construction. The camera keeps reminding us that pop performance is a set of assignments: who gets the voice, who gets the instrument, who gets to look bored. Simon and Chase turn that confusion into the entire point.
angle: The video is a deliberately engineered misidentification machine: it makes the wrong person look like the singer, then keeps revealing the machinery as a joke.
